hints: Look closely at lactic acid, it has two different acidic protons, a carboxylic acid $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and an alcohol $\text{OH}$.
Remember that sodium metal is powerful enough to react with both carboxylic acids and alcohols to release hydrogen.
Consider whether $\text{NaHCO}_3$ and $\text{NaOH}$ are strong enough bases to remove the proton from the alcohol group as well as the carboxylic acid group.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two functional groups**

Lactic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H}$, contains a carboxylic acid group and a secondary alcohol group. We only want to change the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ into $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ and leave the $\text{CH(OH)}$ untouched.

Target change:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{Na}$$

**Test reagent 1, excess Na**

Sodium metal reacts with any $\text{O-H}$ bond to give $\text{H}_2$. With excess, it attacks both groups.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(ONa)CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2$$
So excess Na gives the disodium salt, not sodium lactate. Statement 1 is incorrect.

**Test reagents 2 and 3, weak and strong base**

$\text{NaHCO}_3$ reacts with carboxylic acids but is far too weak a base to deprotonate an alcohol. Even in excess it stops at sodium lactate.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Similarly, $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises the carboxylic acid easily, but $\text{OH}^-$ is not a strong enough base to remove the alcohol proton to any significant extent.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So statements 2 and 3 are correct, even in excess.

**Conclude the combination**

Only 2 and 3 give the desired single sodium salt. That corresponds to the 2 and 3 only combination.

options.A: This states 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Statement 1 fails because excess Na reacts with both the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and the alcohol $\text{OH}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(ONa)CO}_2\text{Na}$, so you do not get pure sodium lactate.
options.B: This states 1 and 2 only are correct. Statement 1 is wrong for the reason above, and statement 3 is actually correct because $\text{NaOH}$ selectively neutralises only the carboxylic acid, so this combination is incomplete and includes a wrong reagent.
options.C: This states 2 and 3 only are correct. Both $\text{NaHCO}_3$ and $\text{NaOH}$ deprotonate the much more acidic carboxylic acid group but leave the alcohol group unchanged, even in excess, giving clean $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{Na}$.
options.D: This states 1 only is correct. Excess Na is the one reagent that cannot be used, as it forms the disodium product by attacking the alcohol as well. It also wrongly excludes the two reagents that do work selectively.
